summary: Explains the need for SIP URI-list services and sets out requirements for invoking them. It also defines a framework for these services, which includes security considerations that apply to them. URI-list services let a client send one request that a server distributes to many recipients. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5363 describes a SIP server that takes one request naming a list of recipients and sends a similar request to each of them. The list can travel inside the request or be stored at the server. The RFC sets out what such a server must do, and spends most of its space on the security rules: the caller has to be authenticated, and no one may be added to a list without having agreed to it first.

questions: send one sip request to many recipients
what is a sip uri-list service
what is the recipient-list content disposition
how do uri-list services prevent amplification attacks
subtitle: How one SIP request can be turned into a request to every member of a list, without overloading the sender's link.

tldr.problem: An application that has to do the same thing to many recipients, such as sending the same instant message to a group, makes one transaction per recipient. On a slow access link that can take a long time, and a single request that names hundreds of recipients can be used to flood a third party.
tldr.mechanism: A URI-list service takes one request that contains or points at a list of URIs and sends a similar request to each of them, behaving as a back-to-back user agent. The list travels in a request body with the new content disposition type recipient-list, or lives at the server. The RFC states the requirements such a service must meet, above all that it authenticate the caller and only send to destinations that agreed in advance to receive such requests.
tldr.outcome: The result is a common framework that the per-method specifications build on, with the fan-out moved off the caller's link and the rules that keep it from becoming an amplifier. The RFC says the mechanism for obtaining consent must be the consent framework of RFC 5360.

today: RFC 5363 is a Proposed Standard from October 2008 and is neither obsoleted nor updated. It defines the recipient-list content disposition type, and it requires URI-list services to implement the consent framework of RFC 5360. The per-method rules that build on it are in RFC 5366 for INVITE, RFC 5365 for MESSAGE and RFC 5367 for SUBSCRIBE.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Some applications need a SIP user agent to perform a similar transaction with a number of remote user agents at a given moment. An instant messaging application that needs to send a particular message, for example "Hello folks", to n receivers needs to send n MESSAGE requests, one to each receiver. When the repeated transaction consists of a large request, or the number of recipients is high, or both, the access network of the user agent has to carry a considerable amount of traffic, and completing all the transactions on a low-bandwidth access would take a long time. That is unacceptable for a number of applications.

The solution introduced in this document is a URI-list service in the network. The task of a URI-list service is to receive a request that contains or references a URI list, that is, a list of one or more URIs, and to send a number of similar requests to the destinations in that list. Once the requests are sent, the service typically informs the user agent about their status. Effectively the URI-list service behaves as a back-to-back user agent.

A URI-list service can take as its input a URI list contained in the SIP request sent by the client, or an external URI list, where the Request-URI is a SIP URI associated with a URI list at the server. External URI lists are typically set up using out-of-band mechanisms, for example the XML Configuration Access Protocol. The RFC gives requirements and a framework for URI-list services using request-contained lists, external lists, or both.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of a program sending a hundred separate messages, it sends one request to a server that holds a list, and the server sends the hundred messages. The sender's link carries one request instead of a hundred, and the server can report back how each one went.

sections.title: Requirements
sections.content:
Two requirements apply to services that use request-contained lists. The first is that the invocation mechanism must allow the invoker to provide a list of destination URIs to the URI-list service. The second is that the invocation mechanism should not require more than one transaction.

Four further requirements apply to all URI-list services. A URI-list service may include services beyond sending requests to the URIs in the list, so it can be modelled as an application server; for example, a service handling INVITE requests may behave as a conference server and mix media for all the participants. The interpretation of the meaning of the URI list sent by the invoker is at the discretion of the application to which the list is sent. It must be possible for the invoker to find out about the result of the operations the service performed with the list, for instance the status of the transactions the service started. And a URI-list service must not send requests to any destination without authenticating the invoker.
sections.plainLanguage: The service must be reachable in a single transaction, must let the caller find out what happened, and must not send anything on behalf of a caller it has not authenticated. What the list means is up to the application that receives it.

sections.title: Carrying URI Lists in SIP
sections.content:
To give a URI-list service a URI list in a single transaction, the RFC defines a new disposition type for the Content-Disposition header field, called recipient-list. Both requests and responses may carry recipient-list bodies, and a body whose disposition type is recipient-list carries a list of URIs that contains the final recipients of the requests to be generated by the service.

The default format for recipient-list bodies is service specific, so specifications for URI-list services must state a default format for the recipient-list bodies used within a particular service. In any case, clients should not include any particular URI more than once in a given URI list.

A server receiving a request with more than one recipient-list body part, for example parts in different URI-list formats, must behave as if it had received a single URI list containing all the URIs present in the different body parts. A server receiving a recipient-list URI list that contains a URI more than once must behave as if that URI appeared in the list only once, using the comparison rules specific to the URI scheme of each URI in the list to decide whether a URI appears more than once. A related document defines a copy-control attribute for resource lists, which can tag duplicated entries with different values; URI-list services that use it have to follow its recommendations about avoiding sending duplicated requests.
sections.plainLanguage: The list travels in the body of the request, marked as a recipient-list, and the format of that body is decided by the service that will use it. If the same address is listed twice, the server treats it as one address and sends one request to it.

sections.title: Processing URI Lists and Reporting Results
sections.content:
Because a URI-list service can behave as an application server, taking a URI list as an input and providing arbitrary services, the way a server interprets a URI list depends on the service to be provided. For a conference server, the URIs in the list may identify the initial set of participants, while for a server dealing with MESSAGE requests they may identify the recipients of an instant message. At the SIP level, the behaviour of application servers receiving requests with URI lists should therefore be specified on a per-service basis, and the RFC names the specifications that do this for INVITE, for MESSAGE and for SUBSCRIBE.

How the user agent finds out about the operations the application server performed is also service specific. A user agent establishing an ad hoc conference with an INVITE carrying a URI list may discover which participants were successfully brought into the conference by using the conference event package.
sections.plainLanguage: What the list means depends on the service: for a conference it names the first participants, for messaging it names the recipients. Each method therefore has its own rules, and each has its own way of telling the caller what happened.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security plays an important role in the implementation of any URI-list service, and it is the most important common area across all types of them. By definition a URI-list service takes one request in and sends a potentially large number out, so attackers may try to use them as traffic amplifiers to launch denial-of-service attacks.

Attackers may also modify URI lists sent from clients to servers, which would cause a different behaviour at the server than the client expected, for example requests being sent to different recipients than the ones specified. To prevent this, clients should integrity protect URI lists with end-to-end mechanisms such as S/MIME, or, if that is not available, hop-by-hop mechanisms such as TLS. Both S/MIME and TLS can also provide confidentiality for the list if that is needed.

The amplification attack itself works like this. An attacker sends a URI list whose host parts route to the victims of the denial-of-service attack, and those victims need not be SIP nodes; they can be non-SIP endpoints or even routers. If the attack succeeds, the attacker can flood a set of nodes, or a single node, with traffic without generating a high volume of traffic itself. The problem is not specific to SIP URI-list services; it also appears in multihoming scenarios where a server has to contact a set of IP addresses provided by a client.

Several measures have to be taken. The first is to keep unauthorized users from using URI-list services at all: a service must not perform any request explosion for an unauthorized user, and must authenticate users and check that they are authorized to request the service before performing any fan-out. The same risk exists when a client uses stored URI lists, so application servers must use authentication and authorization mechanisms with equivalent security properties for stored and request-contained lists.

Authorized users can still cause trouble, so the RFC introduces the concept of opt-in lists. A service should not allow a client to place a user in a URI list unless that user has previously agreed to be placed in such a list, and a service must not send a request to a destination that has not agreed to receive requests from the service beforehand. Users can agree in several ways, such as filling in a web page, sending an email, signing a contract, or using the framework for consent-based communications in SIP. Users must also be able to describe further which requests they are willing to receive, for example only requests from a particular URI-list service on behalf of a particular user.

When a service receives a request with a URI list, it checks whether all the destinations have agreed beforehand to receive requests from the service on behalf of this client. If the list has permission to send requests to all of its targets, it does so, and if not, it sends no request at all. The mechanism used to obtain permissions should not itself create opportunities for amplification: a service must not automatically contact the full set of targets for which it lacks permission, because it would then be receiving one request and sending out a number of authorization request messages. The consent framework avoids this by having the client generate roughly the same amount of traffic towards the service as the service generates towards the destinations, and URI-list services must implement and should use that framework.

Finally, a service may have policies that limit the number of URIs in the lists it accepts, because a very long list could be used in a denial-of-service attack to place a large burden on the service. The recommendations of section 19.1.5 of the SIP specification for forming a request from a URI apply to all URI-list services, and specifications dealing with individual methods must describe the security issues that relate to each particular method.
sections.plainLanguage: One request turning into many is exactly what an attacker wants, so the service has to check who is asking, and only send to people who agreed beforehand to receive such requests. The way that agreement is asked for must not itself become an amplifier.

viz.caption: THE REQUIREMENTS OF A URI-LIST SERVICE

items.title: REQ 1
items.text: The invocation mechanism must allow the invoker to provide a list of destination URIs to the service.

items.title: REQ 2
items.text: The invocation mechanism should not require more than one transaction.

items.title: GEN 1
items.text: A service may provide more than request fan-out, so it can be modelled as an application server.

items.title: GEN 2
items.text: The meaning of the list is at the discretion of the application to which the list is sent.

items.title: GEN 3
items.text: The invoker must be able to find out about the result of the operations the service performed.

items.title: GEN 4
items.text: A service must not send requests to any destination without authenticating the invoker.
